title: What Is Effective Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a compact definition of effective classroom management as the combination of two complementary forces: a fair, unbiased, referee-like accountability system (the classroom management plan) and a genuine, cultivated love of being part of the class, built from purpose, humor, rapport, order, and belonging. He explicitly rules out manipulation, bribery, intimidation, rewards, and one-on-one counseling as producing only temporary suppression of misbehavior rather than real change, positioning the plan-plus-belonging combination as the only path to lasting effectiveness. The piece is written in an unusually lyrical register, comparing the two forces to converging ocean waves that together become irresistible, and frames the definition as the foundational thesis underlying the entire SCM philosophy.
points: Effective classroom management is defined as two complementary forces: fair, unbiased accountability via a plan, plus a genuinely cultivated love of being part of the class.
Common methods like bribery, rewards, threats, and one-on-one counseling are explicitly said to dampen misbehavior only temporarily rather than actually change it.
The classroom management plan itself is described as non-negotiable and unchangeable once taught, deriving its power specifically from being beyond argument.
Purpose, humor, order, rapport, and a feeling of belonging are named as the specific characteristics that build the 'love of being part of the class' force.
quotes: Although these and other common methods can dampen misbehavior temporarily, they don’t actually change it. In fact, they make behavior worse.
Unbiased and non-judgemental, the plan is taught, modeled, and executed as written—the same for every student—by the teacher using referee-like precision, consistency, and calmness.
It needs a force that draws students away from the desire to misbehave and toward the intrinsic desire to improve and succeed. That force is the love of being part of the class.
They awaken and deepen self-worth, natural happiness, and intrinsic motivation to do and be better.
Together, and implemented as we teach here at SCM and in our books, the dual forces are irresistible, like the waves of Nazaré.
